content: Endometriosis is a chronic gynecological condition characterized by the presence of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus, commonly on pelvic organs such as ovaries and peritoneum. This ectopic tissue responds to hormonal cycles similarly to uterine endometrium, leading to inflammation, pain, and formation of scar tissue. The precise cause is multifactorial, involving retrograde menstruation, genetic factors, immune dysregulation, and environmental influences. Symptoms typically include chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea (painful periods), dyspareunia (painful intercourse), and infertility, significantly impacting quality of life. Diagnosis often requires a combination of clinical assessment, imaging, and sometimes laparoscopic surgery to confirm lesions. Management includes hormonal therapies to suppress ectopic tissue activity, pain relief strategies, and surgery for lesion removal or fertility preservation. Endometriosis is a heterogeneous and often underdiagnosed condition with varying presentation severity. Awareness of misdiagnoses, such as confusing it with pelvic inflammatory disease or irritable bowel syndrome, is crucial. Safety considerations include monitoring side effects of hormonal medications and surgical risks. Alternative and complementary therapies are emerging but require further evidence. This module provides a comprehensive overview for patients and healthcare providers to understand, identify, and manage endometriosis effectively.

content: Endometriosis is defined by the growth of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus, commonly on pelvic organs including the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and peritoneal surfaces. It affects approximately 10-15% of reproductive-age women worldwide, though prevalence estimates vary due to diagnostic challenges. The disease is chronic and progressive in many cases, with symptoms ranging from mild to debilitating. Early identification is complicated by overlap with other pelvic pain disorders.

content: The underlying mechanisms of endometriosis involve ectopic implantation of endometrial cells, most commonly explained by Sampson's theory of retrograde menstruation where menstrual blood containing viable endometrial cells flows backward into the pelvic cavity. Other proposed mechanisms include coelomic metaplasia and embryonic cell rests. Immune system dysfunction and inflammation play critical roles, facilitating lesion survival and angiogenesis. Hormonal influences, particularly estrogen dependence, sustain lesion activity and pain.

content: Risk factors for endometriosis include early menarche, shorter menstrual cycles, nulliparity, genetic predisposition, and family history. Environmental exposures such as dioxins and other endocrine disruptors have been investigated but evidence remains moderate. Protective factors may include prolonged breastfeeding and use of combined hormonal contraceptives. Understanding risk profiles aids in early consideration and diagnosis.

content: Patients with endometriosis commonly present with chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea (painful periods), dyspareunia (pain during intercourse), and may experience urinary or gastrointestinal symptoms when lesions involve bladder or bowel. Infertility is also a frequent clinical issue. Symptom severity does not always correlate with lesion extent, and some individuals may be asymptomatic. Pain mechanisms include inflammation, nerve involvement, and adhesions.

content: Diagnosis of endometriosis often begins with detailed history and pelvic examination. Imaging methods like transvaginal ultrasound and MRI can detect endometriomas and deep infiltrating lesions but cannot conclusively identify all endometriosis types. Definitive diagnosis is achieved via laparoscopy with histological confirmation. Non-invasive biomarkers or tests are under investigation but currently lack validation. Delayed diagnosis is common, averaging 7-10 years from symptom onset.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Medical therapies aim to reduce symptoms by suppressing ovarian hormone production to induce a hypoestrogenic state, thus limiting lesion stimulation. Common treatments include combined oral contraceptives, progestins, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists and antagonists, and aromatase inhibitors. Pain management with NSAIDs is also utilized. Medical treatment does not cure endometriosis but helps in symptom control. Side effects and contraindications vary by medication class.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Surgical treatment involves laparoscopic removal or ablation of endometriotic lesions and adhesions to relieve pain and improve fertility outcomes. Surgery may be conservative (organ-sparing) or, in severe cases, more extensive such as hysterectomy. Surgical expertise and patient selection are crucial to minimize complications and recurrence. Surgery can provide significant relief but may not be curative; some patients require adjunctive medical therapies postoperatively.

content: Endometriosis is associated with infertility in up to 30-50% of affected women. Mechanisms include anatomical distortion by adhesions, inflammation impairing oocyte quality, and altered pelvic environment. Treatment depends on disease severity, patient age, and fertility desire, including surgical intervention or assisted reproductive technologies. Fertility counseling is an important component of comprehensive care.

content: Common misconceptions about endometriosis include beliefs that pelvic pain is normal for menstruation, or that endometriosis only occurs in older women. Stigma and normalization of symptoms can delay diagnosis and treatment. Another misconception is that hysterectomy cures endometriosis in all cases, which is not always true. Education and awareness can help counter these misunderstandings and improve patient support.

chunk_title: Lifestyle, Complementary Therapies, and Supportive Care
content: Lifestyle modifications such as regular exercise, diet adjustments, and stress reduction may help manage symptoms but evidence is emerging and limited. Complementary therapies like acupuncture, physical therapy, and dietary supplements have shown potential benefit in some studies but require further high-quality research. Support groups and counseling can provide emotional support, addressing the chronic nature and psychosocial impact of the disease.

content: Safety concerns include monitoring adverse effects of hormonal agents such as bone density reduction with prolonged GnRH agonist use and thromboembolic risk with estrogen-containing therapies. Surgical risks include infection, bleeding, and organ injury. Long-term surveillance and balancing treatment risks vs benefits are essential. Patient education about warning signs and adherence supports safe management.
